entry: Holiday observed on 31 October in many countries, the eve of All Hallows' Day. Also known as All Hallows' Eve or All Saints' Eve, it begins Allhallowtide, a period for remembering saints, martyrs and the faithful departed. Some theories link its customs to the [[Samhain|Samhain]] festival of the [[Celts|Celtic]] harvest, which is believed to have pagan roots, while other scholars say it began independently as a Christian vigil. Celebrated in Ireland and Scotland for centuries, it was carried to North America by Irish and Scottish immigrants in the 19th century. Popular activities include [[Trick-or-treating|trick-or-treating]], costume parties, carving [[Jack-o'-lantern|jack-o'-lanterns]] and telling frightening stories. Some Christians attend church services and light candles on graves, while others treat it as a secular celebration. In popular culture it has become associated with horror and the supernatural.

Sensory perception in the absence of an external stimulus, with a compelling sense of reality. Hallucinations can occur in any sense, and auditory hallucinations are the most common type; they are very common in [[Schizophrenia|schizophrenia]]. They differ from illusions, which distort a real stimulus, and from mental imagery, which is under voluntary control. Hypnagogic hallucinations, which occur as one falls asleep, and hypnopompic hallucinations, which occur on waking, are considered normal. Hallucinations may be associated with drug use, sleep deprivation, [[Psychosis|psychosis]], neurological disorders and [[Delirium tremens|delirium tremens]], and many occur during [[Sleep paralysis|sleep paralysis]]. The English word was introduced in 1646 by the physician Sir Thomas Browne, from the Latin *alucinari*, "to wander in the mind."

American military science fiction video game series and media franchise. It began in November 2001 with *Halo: Combat Evolved*, a launch title for Microsoft's [[Xbox (console)|Xbox]] developed by Bungie. Microsoft established 343 Industries to oversee the series, which was renamed Halo Studios in 2024. Activision now produces Halo games. The remake *Halo: Campaign Evolved* was released in July 2026. The games have sold more than 81 million copies, and the franchise has earned more than $6 billion in sales across novels, films and other media.

Optical phenomenon of rings, arcs and spots of light in the sky, produced by ice crystals. Halos form when light, typically from the [[Sun|Sun]] or [[Moon|Moon]], is refracted and reflected by ice crystals in cirrus or cirrostratus clouds, or in diamond dust near the ground. The most common type is the 22° halo, a circular ring, alongside light pillars and [[Sun dog|sun dogs]]. Halos were long part of weather lore, and they often indicate that rain will fall within 24 hours, because the clouds that cause them can signal an approaching frontal system. The first European descriptions of complex displays date from about 1630.

Organic compound derived from an alkane in which one or more hydrogen atoms are replaced by halogens. Haloalkanes, also called alkyl halides, have the general formula RX, where R is an alkyl group and X is [[Fluorine|fluorine]], [[Chlorine|chlorine]], [[Bromine|bromine]] or [[Iodine|iodine]]. They serve as flame retardants, refrigerants, propellants, solvents and pharmaceuticals. Chlorofluorocarbons, a widely used class, were shown to lead to [[Ozone depletion|ozone depletion]], and haloalkanes containing chlorine, bromine or iodine threaten the ozone layer. Chloro-, bromo- and iodoalkanes have higher melting and boiling points than their parent alkanes. Haloalkanes were known for centuries; chloroethane was produced in the 15th century, and systematic synthesis developed in the 19th century. Substantial amounts are biogenic, produced by living organisms.

Group of chemically related elements in group 17 of the periodic table. The halogens are [[Fluorine|fluorine]], [[Chlorine|chlorine]], [[Bromine|bromine]], [[Iodine|iodine]] and the radioactive [[Astatine|astatine]] and [[Tennessine|tennessine]], although some authors exclude tennessine, whose chemistry is unknown. The name means "salt former," as halogens form salts with metals, such as sodium chloride. All form acids when bonded to hydrogen, and the middle halogens, chlorine, bromine and iodine, are often used as disinfectants. Fluorine was isolated in 1886 by Henri Moissan, while chlorine was first produced in 1774 by Carl Wilhelm Scheele. Iodine was discovered in 1811 by Bernard Courtois, and astatine was produced in 1940.

Decision problem in computability theory. It asks whether a given computer program, run on a given input, will eventually halt or will continue to run forever. [[Alan Turing|Alan Turing]] proved in 1937 that no general [[Algorithm|algorithm]] can solve the problem for all program–input pairs, making it undecidable. The proof constructs a "pathological" program that does the opposite of whatever a supposed halting decider predicts about it. Specific programs can often be shown to halt, and tools such as the T2 Temporal Prover have established that certain device-driver routines always return.

[[Pork|Pork]] from a leg cut that has been preserved by dry or wet curing, with or without smoking. Traces of cured ham appear among the Etruscans of the 6th and 5th centuries BC, and [[Cato the Elder|Cato the Elder]] wrote about salting hams around 160 BC. The word derives from Old English *hamm*, the hollow of the knee, and came to refer to the hind-leg cut around the 15th century. Dry curing uses salt, sometimes with herbs and spices, followed by drying for months; Jinhua ham takes about 8 to 10 months and Iberian ham up to two years. Wet-cured hams are brined. Most modern dry-cured hams use [[Sodium nitrite|sodium nitrite]] or potassium nitrite, which inhibit bacteria and give a red color, though nitrites can form nitrosamines, which are known carcinogens, during cooking.

Sunni Islamist Palestinian political organization with a military wing, the al-Qassam Brigades. Founded in 1987 during the First Intifada, it won a majority in the 2006 legislative election and has governed the [[Gaza Strip|Gaza Strip]] since seizing it in 2007. Israel and Egypt imposed blockades, and wars followed, the latest ongoing since the [[October 7 attacks|October 7 attacks]] of 2023. Its 1988 charter was widely described as antisemitic; a 2017 charter supported a Palestinian state within the 1967 borders, and it is debated whether this reflects a policy change. Several governments, including the United States and the European Union, designate it a terrorist organization, a label Hamas rejects.

City-state in northern Germany, the second-largest city in the country after [[Berlin|Berlin]]. Its port is Germany's largest and Europe's third-largest, after [[Rotterdam|Rotterdam]] and Antwerp, and the Elbe estuary begins in the city. Hamburg was a member of the [[Hanseatic League|Hanseatic League]], and its name derives from a castle that [[Charlemagne|Charlemagne]] ordered built in AD 808. The city recovered from the Great Fire of 1842, Allied bombing in 1943 and the North Sea flood of 1962. It is home to Airbus, Lufthansa, Unilever and Germany's oldest stock exchange. Its Speicherstadt and Kontorhausviertel were declared [[World Heritage Site|World Heritage Sites]] by UNESCO in 2015. Hamburg has about 2,500 bridges, more than any other European city, and it is known for the Elbphilharmonie concert hall and the Reeperbahn district.

Sandwich of a patty of panfried or grilled ground meat, typically [[Beef|beef]], in a sliced bun. Burgers are commonly topped with lettuce, tomato, onion, pickles and condiments such as [[Ketchup|ketchup]] or mustard, and served with [[French fries|French fries]]. The name probably derives from the German city of [[Hamburg|Hamburg]], although the connection is disputed. A recipe for "Hamburgh sausage" appeared in a 1758 cookbook, and the *Chicago Daily Tribune* described a "hamburger sandwich" in 1896. Several people, including Charlie Nagreen and Louis Lassen, have been credited with inventing it, and its origin remains unclear. [[Fast food|Fast-food]] chains made the hamburger a staple, and McDonald's Big Mac and Burger King's Whopper are global icons of American culture.

Port city in southern Ontario, Canada (pop., 2021: 569,353), at the western end of [[Lake Ontario|Lake Ontario]]. It lies about 68 km southwest of [[Toronto|Toronto]]. Conceived by George Hamilton after the [[War of 1812|War of 1812]], it became the center of the industrialized Golden Horseshoe region. The economy was long led by steel and heavy manufacturing, and since the 2010s services such as health and science have grown. Its present boundaries date from amalgamation on January 1, 2001. The city is home to McMaster University, the Royal Botanical Gardens and the Canadian Warplane Heritage Museum. Its residents are known as Hamiltonians.

Sung-and-rapped-through biographical musical by [[Lin-Manuel Miranda|Lin-Manuel Miranda]], based on Ron Chernow's 2004 biography. It traces the life of [[Alexander Hamilton|Alexander Hamilton]] from the [[American Revolution|American Revolution]] to his fatal duel with Aaron Burr. Its score draws on hip hop, R&B, pop and soul, and it casts non-white actors as the Founding Fathers. It opened off-Broadway on February 17, 2015, and on Broadway that August. At the 70th Tony Awards it won 11 awards, including Best Musical, and it won the 2016 [[Pulitzer Prize|Pulitzer Prize]] for Drama. Productions have played in [[London|London]] and [[Hamburg|Hamburg]], and a filmed version was released on Disney+ in 2020.

Reformulation of [[Classical mechanics|classical mechanics]] based on momenta rather than velocities. Introduced by [[William Rowan Hamilton|Sir William Rowan Hamilton]] in 1833, it replaces the generalized velocities of [[Lagrangian mechanics|Lagrangian mechanics]] with generalized momenta, though both describe the same physical phenomena. The Hamiltonian is the energy function of the system, which in simple cases is the sum of [[Kinetic energy|kinetic]] and [[Potential energy|potential energy]]. Hamilton's equations describe the motion as first-order differential equations in phase space. A spherical pendulum, a mass moving without friction on a sphere under gravity, is a standard worked example. The approach has a close relationship with symplectic geometry and serves as a link between classical and [[Quantum mechanics|quantum mechanics]].

Tragedy by [[William Shakespeare|William Shakespeare]], written around 1599–1601 and set in Denmark. Prince Hamlet seeks revenge on his uncle Claudius, who has murdered Hamlet's father, seized the throne and married Hamlet's mother, Gertrude. Hamlet feigns madness, and his soliloquies, including "To be, or not to be," probe death, suicide and hesitation. The play ends in widespread death, including Hamlet's own. Possible sources range from ancient Greek tragedies to Elizabethan dramas, including the lost *Ur-Hamlet* attributed to Thomas Kyd. Three early versions survive: the First Quarto of 1603, the Second Quarto of 1604 and the First Folio of 1623. It is widely considered one of the greatest plays ever written.

Hand tool with a weighted head fixed to a long handle, swung to deliver an impact. Hammers drive nails into wood, shape metal and crush rock, and are associated with [[Carpentry|carpentry]], blacksmithing and warfare. The modern head is usually heat-treated steel, and the handle, or haft, is typically wood or plastic. The claw hammer, a household staple in North America, has a claw for pulling out [[Nail (fastener)|nails]]. Over 40 types exist, including sledgehammers, mallets and ball-peen hammers, and powered hammers such as steam hammers deliver forces beyond the human arm. Simple hammers date to about 3.3 million years ago, when stones were used to strike wood, bone and other stones near [[Lake Turkana|Lake Turkana]] in [[Kenya|Kenya]]. Handles were added by about 30,000 BCE, giving the user better control.

Shark of the family Sphyrnidae, with a flattened, T-shaped head called a cephalofoil. The eyes sit at the ends of the head, which gives superior binocular vision and depth perception and increases the surface for electroreceptors. Hammerheads live worldwide in warm coastal waters and on [[Continental shelf|continental shelves]]. Unlike most sharks, some species form large schools by day and hunt alone at night. The great hammerhead, the largest species, averages 4.0 m (13.1 ft) in length, and the bonnethead is the smallest. Their closest relatives are the requiem sharks, and [[Fossil|fossils]] of the family date to the Eocene. Most species are threatened by fishing, and the great and scalloped hammerheads are rated [[Endangered species|critically endangered]].

Ceremonial county in South East England (pop., 2024: 1,920,959), bordered by the Solent to the south. Its largest settlement is [[Southampton|Southampton]], and the city of Portsmouth lies in the south-east. Chalk hills cross the county, and the New Forest holds one of England's largest expanses of ancient woodland. Hampshire's recorded history begins in Roman Britain, when its chief town was Venta Belgarum, now Winchester. The [[Domesday Book|Domesday Book]] divided the county into 44 hundreds. Its ports played a crucial military role in both world wars. Colonists who left Hampshire for North America named [[New Hampshire|New Hampshire]] after their homeland.

Small [[Rodent|rodent]] of the subfamily Cricetinae, widely kept as a [[Pet|pet]]. The subfamily contains 19 species in seven genera, within a family that also includes [[Vole|voles]], [[Lemming|lemmings]] and [[Muskrat|muskrats]]. The best-known species is the golden or Syrian hamster, *Mesocricetus auratus*, the type most commonly kept as a pet. Three dwarf species, including the Roborovski hamster and the winter white Djungarian hamster, are also kept. Hamsters eat seeds, fruits, vegetation and occasionally insects. In the wild they forage at twilight, while in captivity they live a conventionally nocturnal life. Their elongated cheek pouches carry food back to their burrows. The earliest hamsters appeared in the Middle [[Miocene|Miocene]], about 15 million years ago. The name is a loanword from German.

East Asian ethnic group native to Greater China, the largest ethnic group in the world. With a population of over 1.4 billion, Han Chinese make up about 17% of the world population, including 91.11% of the population of [[China|China]] and 97% of that of [[Taiwan|Taiwan]]. They form a significant diaspora in Southeast Asia, including Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Myanmar, Vietnam, the Philippines and Indonesia. They trace their ancestry to the Huaxia, agricultural tribes along the middle and lower reaches of the [[Yellow River|Yellow River]]. Migration during the [[Qin dynasty|Qin]] (221–206 BC) and [[Han dynasty|Han]] (202 BC–AD 220) dynasties spread Han people southward, and the name "Han people" was inspired by the Han dynasty. The [[Chinese language|Chinese language]] is also called the Han language.

Chinese [[Legalism (Chinese philosophy)|Legalist]] philosopher and statesman of the Warring States period. Han Fei was an imperial clansman of the state of Han and is often considered the greatest representative of Legalism. The anthology *Han Feizi*, traditionally attributed to him, synthesized the methods of his predecessors. He borrowed Shang Yang's emphasis on laws, Shen Buhai's administrative technique and Shen Dao's ideas on authority, and stressed the ruler's control through power, technique and law. His ideas are sometimes compared with those of [[Niccolò Machiavelli|Niccolò Machiavelli]], author of *The Prince*. He went to the state of [[Qin dynasty|Qin]], where, according to [[Sima Qian|Sima Qian]], he was imprisoned and died by suicide. Legalism was later vilified by the [[Han dynasty|Han dynasty]], yet its ideas continued to influence every dynasty thereafter.

Chinese essayist, Confucian scholar and poet of the [[Tang dynasty|Tang dynasty]]. Han Yu led a revolt against the ornate parallel prose of his time and advocated a simple, logical style called *guwen*, or "ancient writing," which he saw as suited to restoring Confucianism. He is often considered among China's finest prose writers, and the [[Ming dynasty|Ming dynasty]] scholar Mao Kun ranked him first among the Eight Great Prose Masters of the Tang and Song. He opposed Buddhism, and in 819 he submitted a memorial protesting the court's preparations to receive a Buddha's finger bone relic. He was saved from execution, then demoted and exiled to Chaozhou. Later he returned to the capital and held high posts, including rector of the Imperial University. His essays influenced later Neo-Confucian thinkers.

Prehensile, multi-fingered appendage at the end of the forelimb in tetrapods, used mainly for grasping and manipulating objects. The only true grasping hands occur in the mammalian order of [[Primate|primates]], which have opposable thumbs. The human hand has five digits and 27 bones, excluding a variable sesamoid bone. Fingers have some of the densest nerve endings in the body and provide the richest source of tactile feedback. Hands play a role in [[Body language|body language]] and [[Sign language|sign language]], and the ten digits of two hands helped give rise to number systems. Some animals, such as the [[Koala|koala]] and [[Giant panda|giant panda]], are described as having hands although they are not true grasping hands. In comparative anatomy the digited part of any forelimb is called the manus.

Common infection caused by a group of enteroviruses, mostly affecting children under five. It typically begins with fever and malaise, followed a day or two later by flat spots or blisters on the hands, feet and mouth, and sometimes the buttocks and groin. Coxsackievirus A16 is the most common cause, and enterovirus 71 the second most common. Infection spreads through close contact, coughing and feces, and childcare settings are common sites of outbreaks. Most cases resolve on their own within 7 to 10 days, and no antiviral medication or [[Vaccine|vaccine]] is available. [[Ibuprofen|Ibuprofen]] may be used for fever and mouth pain, but aspirin should be avoided in children. Rarely, viral [[Meningitis|meningitis]] or [[Encephalitis|encephalitis]] may complicate the disease.

Method of turning fibers such as [[Wool|wool]], [[Flax|flax]] or cotton into [[Yarn|yarn]] by hand, one of the oldest textile arts. Fibers were drawn out and twisted with simple tools, the spindle and distaff. A weight called a spindle whorl, first used in the [[Neolithic|Neolithic]] era, helped the spindle rotate steadily. Evidence of spinning, including depictions of string skirts, dates to the [[Upper Paleolithic|Upper Paleolithic]] era, some 20,000 years ago. The spinning wheel reached Europe by the 13th century and greatly increased the output of individual spinners. Hand spinning was a household task, and "spinster" came to mean an unmarried woman. Mechanical methods during the [[Industrial Revolution|Industrial Revolution]] made it uneconomic, but it survives as a popular [[Handicraft|handicraft]].
